note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in MN.json, gathered 2026-10-04 (MnDOT, Explore Minnesota, byway organizations and Wikipedia).

byways.name: Apple Blossom Drive Scenic Byway
byways.where: County Highway 29 and connecting county roads from La Crescent north through Dakota and Nodine to US 61 (Great River Road); southeast Minnesota

facts.fact: The byway follows county roads (County Highway 29) from La Crescent north to Highway 61, and each end connects with the Great River Road; Explore Minnesota gives its length as 19 miles, while Visit Bluff Country gives 17 miles.
The route runs on bluff tops above the Mississippi River valley and is accessible from La Crescent, Dakota and Nodine.
Great River Bluffs State Park on the route has overlooks of the Mississippi valley, and orchards along the drive sell apples, cider and pumpkins.

byways.name: Avenue of Pines Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 46 between Deer River (US 2) and Northome (MN 1), through Squaw Lake; Itasca County, Chippewa National Forest

facts.fact: The byway runs 46 miles on Highway 46 between Deer River and Northome.

Views include mature red pine stands and lakes including Cut Foot Sioux and Lake Winnibigoshish, Minnesota's fifth-largest lake; the corridor alternates between enclosed pine forest and open views near water and marsh.
Highway 46 was authorized in 1933 and completely paved by 1958; it passes through the Chippewa National Forest in Itasca County.

byways.name: Edge of the Wilderness National Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 38 from Grand Rapids (US 2) north through Marcell and Bigfork to Effie (MN 1); Itasca County, Chippewa National Forest

facts.fact: The byway follows Highway 38 for 47 miles between Grand Rapids and Effie, a route once used by voyageurs and loggers through the Chippewa National Forest, over rolling hills and past bogs and fishing lakes.
A hiking trail off the byway leads to the old Joyce Estate, once a millionaire's vacation hideaway.
The entire length of Highway 38 is designated a National Scenic Byway; the highway was authorized in 1933 and completely paved by 1940.

byways.name: Glacial Ridge Trail Scenic Byway
byways.where: Loops of MN 9, 23, 29, 55, 104, US 71 and county roads between Willmar and Glenwood, with extensions to Alexandria and Sauk Centre; west central Minnesota

facts.fact: The byway is 245 miles of loops in the countryside between Willmar and Glenwood, with extensions to Alexandria and Sauk Centre.
Melting glaciers left the region dotted with lakes among hills and ridges, and the route passes lakes, woods, prairie and farmland.
Three state parks lie on the route: Sibley, Monson Lake and Glacial Lakes, with hardwood forest, prairie and lakes.

byways.name: Grand Rounds National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Loop of parkways around Minneapolis (Chain of Lakes, Minnehaha, Mississippi River, Northeast, Victory Memorial, Theodore Wirth and Downtown Riverfront segments); Hennepin County

facts.fact: The Grand Rounds includes approximately 55 miles of parkways in seven segments, the longest being the 13.3-mile Chain of Lakes segment.
It was originally conceived by Horace W. S. Cleveland in the early days of the Minneapolis park system, designated a Minnesota State Scenic Byway in 1997 and a National Scenic Byway in April 1998.
Landmarks along the loop include the waterfall in Minnehaha Park, the rose garden at Lake Harriet and the Stone Arch Bridge, built in 1883.

byways.name: Great River Road All-American Scenic Byway
byways.where: Network of US, state and county roads (including US 61, US 10, US 2 and MN 371) along the Mississippi from Itasca State Park through Bemidji, Grand Rapids, St. Cloud and the Twin Cities to Red Wing, Wabasha and Winona

facts.fact: Minnesota's Great River Road is a designated All-American Road spanning 565 miles, 43 communities, 20 counties and three tribes, marked by a green and white pilot's wheel sign.
Travelers can cross the river's source in Itasca State Park, and Bemidji, the first city on the Mississippi, has statues of Paul Bunyan and Babe.
In the south the river widens through a valley below tall wooded bluffs, past the river towns of Red Wing, Lake City, Wabasha and Winona.

byways.name: Gunflint Trail National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Cook County Road 12 (CSAH 12) from Grand Marais on Lake Superior northwest to Saganaga Lake near the Canadian border; Superior National Forest

facts.fact: The Gunflint Trail is a 57-mile paved road from Grand Marais on Lake Superior's north shore to Saganaga Lake near the Canadian border.
Originally a footpath, it was improved into a dirt road by Cook County in the 1890s; it is named for the spark-producing chert French explorers found at Gunflint Lake.
The Ham Lake Fire of spring 2007 burned over 40,000 acres along the upper Gunflint Trail and destroyed almost 200 structures.

byways.name: Historic Bluff Country National Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 16 between La Crescent and Dexter, with a small loop on US 52 and MN 80 connecting Wykoff and Fountain; Root River valley, southeast Minnesota

facts.fact: The byway is an 88-mile route on Minnesota Highway 16 between Dexter and La Crescent.
It follows the Root River valley among dolomite bluffs, pastures and fields; trout streams run through the region and Amish buggies are a common sight on its country roads.
Attractions include naturalist-guided tours of Mystery Cave and Historic Forestville, where costumed interpreters depict life in 1899.

byways.name: Historic Highway 75 "King of Trails"
byways.where: US 75 the full length of Minnesota near the western border, from the Iowa line south of Luverne through Pipestone, Canby, Breckenridge, Moorhead and Crookston to the Canadian border near Noyes

facts.fact: The byway follows Highway 75 near the western border of the state for the entire length of Minnesota, through gentle prairies and farmland; Explore Minnesota gives its length as 414 miles.
All 408 miles of US 75 in Minnesota are designated the Historic King of Trails, the auto trail name the road carried before the state trunk highway system was commissioned in 1920.

byways.name: Lady Slipper Scenic Byway
byways.where: County Road 39 (with connecting county roads) between Blackduck and US 2 near Cass Lake, about 20 miles east of Bemidji; Chippewa National Forest

facts.fact: The 28-mile byway follows Highway 39 between Blackduck and Highway 2 through the Chippewa National Forest and crosses the Mississippi River.
Lady slipper orchids are common along the route and typically bloom from late June.

The Rabideau CCC Camp off County Highway 39, built 1935 to 1941, keeps 13 of its original 25 buildings, including the mess hall and five barracks, and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2006.

byways.name: Lake Country Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 34 from Detroit Lakes through Park Rapids to Walker, plus US 71 north from Park Rapids to Itasca State Park

facts.fact: The 88-mile byway runs along State Highway 34 from Detroit Lakes to Park Rapids to Walker, with Highway 71 north of Park Rapids to Itasca State Park; it was designated a state byway on May 26, 1999.
The route crosses a transition from prairie grassland in the west to hardwood and conifer forest in the east, and showy lady's slippers bloom in June along the south side of Highway 34.
Itasca State Park at the headwaters of the Mississippi, Tamarac National Wildlife Refuge and hundreds of lakeside resorts lie along the byway.

byways.name: Lake Mille Lacs Scenic Byway
byways.where: Loop around Lake Mille Lacs on US 169, MN 27, MN 18, MN 47 and Shakopee Lake Road, through Garrison, Isle, Wahkon, Onamia and Malmo

facts.fact: The byway is a 68-mile paved loop on Highways 169, 27, 18 and 47 and Shakopee Lake Road, about 90 miles north of Minneapolis-St. Paul; Lake Mille Lacs offers more than 132,500 acres of frozen lake for fishing and kiteboarding in winter.
It was designated Minnesota's 22nd scenic byway and connects Isle, Wahkon, Onamia, Garrison and Malmo.
Stops include the Mille Lacs Indian Museum and Trading Post in Vineland, Mille Lacs Kathio and Father Hennepin state parks, and the sunrise view from the Garrison Concourse.

byways.name: Minnesota River Valley National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Series of US, state and county roads (including US 212, US 169, MN 19, MN 67 and MN 68) following the Minnesota River from Browns Valley and Big Stone Lake through New Ulm, Mankato and St. Peter to Belle Plaine

facts.fact: The 300-mile byway is a series of roads following the Minnesota River from Browns Valley, near Big Stone Lake where the river begins, to Belle Plaine southwest of Minneapolis.
State historic sites along the route include the Lower Sioux Agency, Fort Ridgely and Lac qui Parle Mission, along with sites related to the 1862 U.S.-Dakota War.
The byway organization presents the valley as a 'river of stories,' with sections on the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, the Dakota homeland and natural history.

byways.name: North Shore All-American Scenic Drive
byways.where: County Road 61 (old Highway 61) from Duluth to Two Harbors, then MN 61 along Lake Superior to Grand Portage

facts.fact: The 154-mile All-American Road runs from Duluth to Two Harbors on County Road 61 (old Highway 61), then from Two Harbors to Grand Portage on Highway 61.
The route passes eight state parks, and Minnesota's largest waterfalls are at Grand Portage and Tettegouche state parks.
Split Rock Lighthouse was built after the Mataafa Storm of 1905, first lit on July 31, 1910, and stands on a 133-foot cliff; the Coast Guard retired the light in 1969.

byways.name: Otter Trail Scenic Byway
byways.where: 150-mile loop in Otter Tail County on US 59, MN 78, MN 108, MN 210 and county roads through Fergus Falls, Pelican Rapids, Perham and Battle Lake

facts.fact: The byway is a 150-mile circular drive connecting Fergus Falls, Pelican Rapids, Perham and Battle Lake in Otter Tail County, a region of more than 1,000 lakes.
Stops include Maplewood and Glendalough state parks and the scenic overlook at Inspiration Peak.
Phelps Mill, a flour mill on the Otter Tail River near Underwood, was built in 1888 to 1889, closed in 1939 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.

byways.name: Paul Bunyan National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Double loop of county roads (plus MN 84) between Pequot Lakes and Crosslake, with Pine River, about 30 miles north of Brainerd; two counties

facts.fact: The byway stretches along 54 miles of county roads with broad paved shoulders and spans two counties.
It is a double-circle route between Pequot Lakes and Crosslake, about 30 miles north of Brainerd, named for the legendary lumberjack whose footprints are said to have made the area's lakes.
The Pequot Lakes water tower is painted to look like Paul Bunyan's fishing bobber.

byways.name: Saint Croix Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 95, US 8, MN 23 and county roads along the St. Croix River from Point Douglas near Hastings north to a point beyond Sandstone; Pine County in the north

facts.fact: The 124-mile byway runs from Point Douglas, near Hastings, to a point north of Sandstone.

It follows the St. Croix valley, one of the eight original National Wild and Scenic Rivers, with long views and rolling terrain in the south giving way to rock formations, cliffs and woodland to the north.
The byway organization divides the route into the Stagecoach Trail, Sawmill, Immigrant Trail, Nevers Place and White Pines districts.

byways.name: Shooting Star Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 56 from I-90 south and east through Rose Creek, Adams, Taopi and Le Roy to US 63 near the Iowa line; Mower County

facts.fact: The byway follows Highway 56 for about 31 miles between I-90 and Highway 63 near the Iowa border, east of Austin.
It is one of the state's first designated wildflower routes, and the Minnesota departments of Transportation and Natural Resources manage wildflowers and native grasses along it.
The byway is named for wildflowers that bloom in June and July, and passes through Le Roy, Adams, Taopi and Rose Creek, near Lake Louise State Park.

byways.name: Skyline Drive
byways.where: Skyline Parkway, about 28 miles across the hills of Duluth from Becks Road to Seven Bridges Road; St. Louis County

facts.fact: Skyline Parkway runs 28 miles from Becks Road to Seven Bridges Road and follows the ancient shoreline of Glacial Lake Duluth.
Construction began in April 1889, and in 1894 the Duluth park board named the road Rogers Boulevard after William K. Rogers.
Hawk Ridge, at the northern end of the byway, is a vantage point for watching migratory birds in spring and fall.

byways.name: Superior National Forest Scenic Byway
byways.where: St. Louis County Highways 16, 110 and 135 and Lake County Highways 15 and 5 (with US 53) from the Iron Range towns of Aurora and Hoyt Lakes to Silver Bay on Lake Superior

facts.fact: The 78-mile byway follows Lake County Highways 5 and 15, St. Louis County Highways 16, 110 and 135 and US 53, connecting Aurora, Hoyt Lakes, Eveleth, Gilbert, Biwabik and Silver Bay between the Iron Range and Lake Superior's North Shore.
Landmarks include the 1913 Toimi School, a one-room Finnish immigrant schoolhouse, and the Timber Arch Bridge in Hoyt Lakes.
Hardwoods along the route turn red and yellow in autumn among the pines of the Superior National Forest.

byways.name: Veterans Evergreen Memorial Drive
byways.where: MN 23 from I-35 near Banning and Askov through Bruno, Kerrick, Duquette, Nickerson and Wrenshall to the Gary-New Duluth neighborhood of Duluth; Pine, Carlton and St. Louis counties

facts.fact: The 50-mile byway follows Highway 23, for decades called 'the scenic route to Duluth,' from the Banning exit through Askov, Bruno, Kerrick, Duquette, Nickerson and Wrenshall.
The Nemadji and South Fork rivers on the northern part are known for trout fishing, and the route ends at the Veterans Memorial Overlook above the St. Louis River valley.

The designated segment of MN 23 runs through Pine, Carlton and St. Louis counties, and its bridge over the St. Louis River at Fond du Lac was dedicated in 2008 as the Biauswah Bridge in honor of American Indian veterans.

byways.name: Waters of the Dancing Sky Scenic Byway
byways.where: MN 11 from International Falls west through Baudette and Warroad toward the North Dakota line, with US 59 north to Lake Bronson State Park; along the Canadian border

facts.fact: The 229-mile byway runs mostly on Highway 11 across the top of Minnesota between International Falls and the North Dakota border, following the Rainy River from International Falls to Baudette.
The 'Dancing Sky' refers to the aurora borealis, which frequently appears in the area, and Zippel Bay State Park has a 3-mile beach on Lake of the Woods.
State Highway 11 was authorized in 1920 from Donaldson east to International Falls, and its last unpaved section, near the North Dakota line, was paved by 1961.
